policies.name: PLI scheme for automobiles and auto components
policies.what: Pays incentives on sales of advanced automotive technology products made in India. Outlay ₹25,938 crore; 82 approved applicants (30 Nov 2025); ₹1,350.83 crore paid to five applicants; sales of ₹32,879 crore achieved by 30 Sep 2025 against an eligible-sales target of ₹2,31,500 crore until March 2028.
policies.sourceName: Ministry of Heavy Industries, on PIB

policies.name: PM E-DRIVE
policies.what: Electric vehicle demand incentives, e-buses and public charging. Launched September 2024, extended to 31 March 2028. Outlay ₹11,900 crore (see conflicts). 26.59 lakh EVs sold as of June 2026 against an incentive-supported target of about 28.30 lakh. ₹4,391 crore for 14,028 e-buses; ₹2,000 crore earmarked for charging.
policies.sourceName: Government factsheet, as reported by DD News

policies.name: Wider manufacturing push
policies.what: The government lists PLI schemes, PM GatiShakti, the National Logistics Policy and BHAVYA among its measures to strengthen manufacturing and diversify supply chains.
policies.sourceName: Lok Sabha reply, as reported by ANI

policies.name: Vision 2030 (NITI Aayog)
policies.what: Goal of US$145 billion in production, US$60 billion in exports, and a rise in India's global component trade share from 3% to 8%.

policies.name: GST cut on vehicles (September 2025)
policies.what: GST on small cars and bikes up to 350cc fell from 28% to 18%; large cars moved to a flat 40% with no cess; auto parts also got lower rates. The ministry expects cheaper vehicles to lift demand and orders to component makers.
policies.sourceName: Ministry of Heavy Industries, on PIB

policies.name: Rare-earth magnet scheme (November 2025)
policies.what: ₹7,280 crore to build 6,000 tonnes a year of magnet-making capacity: ₹6,450 crore sales incentive over five years plus ₹750 crore capital subsidy, shared by five winners of up to 1,200 tonnes each. India's magnet use is expected to double by 2030 and is met mainly by imports today.

policies.name: PLI Auto: the rules
policies.what: Cabinet approved it on 15 September 2021. It covers 19 vehicle categories and 103 components, and applicants must reach 50% domestic value addition to qualify. By Dec 2024 only ₹322 crore had been paid.
policies.sourceName: Ministry of Heavy Industries, on PIB

policies.name: Vehicle scrappage policy (2021)
policies.what: A voluntary programme to retire old, unfit vehicles through registered scrapping centres, with fitness tests for commercial vehicles and non-renewal of registration for private ones. Expected to bring about ₹10,000 crore of investment and 35,000 jobs.
policies.sourceName: Ministry of Road Transport, on PIB

drivers: Record domestic demand: all four vehicle segments hit their highest-ever sales in FY2025-26 (SIAM).
Cheaper vehicles: the September 2025 GST cut took small cars and bikes from 28% to 18% (PIB).
Exports are rising fast: passenger +17.5%, two-wheelers +23.4%, three-wheelers +50.1% (SIAM).
Policy support through PLI and PM E-DRIVE, which together channel crores into manufacturing and EVs.
EV adoption: 24.5 lakh EVs registered in FY2025-26, up 25%, and electric two-wheelers reached 6.54% of two-wheeler sales (Vahan).
Localisation: the PLI scheme requires 50% domestic value addition, which pushes more of the supply chain to be built in India (PIB).
A huge job base and supplier network: over 3.5 crore people depend on the industry, which keeps policy attention high (PIB).
Replacement demand: the scrappage policy aims to retire old vehicles and bring in newer, cleaner ones (PIB).

players.structure: A few large vehicle makers buy from a very large component base: component makers supplied ₹6,62,893 crore to vehicle makers in FY2025-26 (ACMA). Maruti Suzuki alone held 41.2% of the domestic passenger vehicle market in Q1 FY2026-27 (company results). The names below are approved PLI applicants, not a ranking by size.

challenges: Component trade gap: imports (US$25.4 billion) exceeded exports (US$24 billion) in FY2025-26 (ACMA).
India holds only about 3% of globally traded auto components, so most of that trade is elsewhere (NITI Aayog).
PLI progress is slow so far: ₹1,350.83 crore paid against a ₹25,938 crore outlay, and only two of ACMA's nearly 1,100 members have received PLI benefits (PIB, ACMA).
Manufacturing's share of GVA is flat at 14.8% (14.7% in 2022-23) despite 10.7% growth (Lok Sabha reply).
US tariffs: the US takes 26% of component exports and nearly half of those face a 25% tariff, with US probes into labour practices and overcapacity still open (ACMA).
Magnet dependence: India's demand for rare-earth magnets is met mainly by imports, and the new scheme will take about 7 years to deliver (PIB).
The EV push is behind plan: 26.59 lakh EVs sold under PM E-DRIVE against a target of about 28.30 lakh (DD News).
ACMA lists geopolitical developments, supply chain disruptions and raw material volatility as risks to watch.
opsAngle: Component supply moves with vehicle output: OEM supplies rose 16.3% to ₹6,62,893 crore, so capacity, inventory and delivery frequency at suppliers have to scale with record vehicle volumes.

Sourcing and localisation: imports exceed exports in components, and the PLI's 50% domestic value addition rule pushes makers to localise parts. Expect questions on make-versus-buy and supplier development.
Export-readiness: vehicle exports are growing fast, yet India's share of traded components is about 3%, so quality, cost and delivery performance decide whether more of that trade can be won.
Single-source risk: rare-earth magnets come mainly from imports, so a good answer mentions dual sourcing, safety stock and the ₹7,280 crore plan to build 6,000 tonnes of local capacity.
Customer concentration: with 26% of component exports going to the US and about half of that facing a 25% tariff, suppliers need pricing clauses, cost pass-through and a plan to win other markets.
Demand shocks: a GST cut from 28% to 18% changes vehicle prices overnight, so planners must flex production schedules, dealer stock and supplier call-offs quickly.
Product mix is shifting: with electric two-wheelers at 6.54% of sales and growing, plants need flexible lines and suppliers need new skills in batteries and motors.
End-of-life flows: the scrappage policy creates reverse logistics and recycled raw materials, which is a growing supply chain topic worth a sentence in a GD.

gdQuestions: India's component imports are higher than exports: is localisation the answer, and what would it cost?
Record vehicle sales but a flat manufacturing share of GVA: is auto really lifting Indian manufacturing?
Should the government keep paying PLI incentives when disbursement is this slow?
Was the 2025 GST cut the main reason sales hit a record, and what happens to demand when that boost fades?
India's magnet supply depends mainly on imports: should it spend ₹7,280 crore to build capacity, or secure long-term supply deals instead?
About half of component exports to the US face a 25% tariff: should suppliers diversify markets or negotiate with the US?
Only two of ACMA's nearly 1,100 members have received PLI benefits: is the scheme built for big players only?
Electric two-wheelers are 6.5% of sales, but PM E-DRIVE is below its target: is India's EV push a success or a miss?
The industry supports over 3.5 crore jobs: how should plants balance automation with employment?
Should vehicle makers make batteries and motors themselves, or buy them from specialists?
conflicts: NITI Aayog summary on PIB: one line says the auto sector gives 7.1% of 'global GDP', while the body says 7.1% of 'India's GDP'. The recap uses the body wording; treat the 7.1% as needing care before quoting.
PM E-DRIVE outlay: the government factsheet reported by DD News (1 Oct 2026) says ₹11,900 crore; earlier reports and the launch coverage said ₹10,900 crore. Shown as ₹11,900 crore with this note.

Logistics cost as a share of GDP: a KPMG blog (Jan 2026) quotes recent government assessments of about 8%; another report (Business Standard, not opened) puts it near 10 to 10.7%; older figures were 13 to 14%. No single figure is shown.

Electric vehicle registrations in FY2025-26: Autocar Professional (Vahan data, 2 Apr 2026) gives 2.45 million; other reports gave 2.55 million and 2.66 million, probably counted differently or at other dates. The recap uses 2.45 million.

Foreign investment: Invest India gives US$37.85 billion for April 2000 to March 2025. A search result showed about US$40.3 billion to March 2026, but the DPIIT file could not be opened to confirm it, so it is not shown.
US share of component exports: ACMA's statement gives 26%; one search result said 27%. The recap uses 26%.
notFound: ACMA's FY2027 growth outlook: seen only in a headline, not in an opened page.
India's total vehicle production in FY2025-26: the SIAM page was read, but the production line could not be confirmed, so only FY2024-25 production (Invest India) is shown.
How many vehicles have been scrapped under the scrappage policy so far: no current official figure was found.

industries.name: FMCG and retail
industries.overview: FMCG (fast-moving consumer goods) is everyday packaged stuff: soap, shampoo, tea, biscuits, noodles. Companies make it in bulk and push it through distributors to millions of small shops, and increasingly to supermarkets and quick-commerce apps. It matters because volume, price and channel mix decide who wins, and every one of them is a supply chain problem.
industries.bigIdea: Indian FMCG is a distribution game that is changing channels fast: volumes were weak in April-June 2026 (down 2%) while modern trade and online grew, so winning means serving the corner shop and the dark store at once.

flow.label: Make
flow.note: Factories and food processors scale up, helped by the food processing PLI scheme (FY2025-26 sales, PIB).

flow.label: Distribute
flow.note: Stockists and wholesalers feed small shops across the country (ITC, FY26).

flow.label: Sell
flow.note: Corner shops are shrinking in volume while modern trade is up 17.5% (NielsenIQ, Q2 2026).

flow.label: Fast channels
flow.note: Online and quick commerce grow far faster than the market, forcing smaller packs and dark-store supply (NielsenIQ, Q2 2026).

drivers: Tax relief for households: no income tax up to ₹12 lakh and cheaper everyday goods under the new GST rates (PIB).
GST cut to 5% on soap, shampoo, toothpaste, ghee, noodles and more, which lowers shelf prices on staples (GST Council release).
Premiumisation and market development: HUL says premium soaps, bodywash and liquids grew double digit (HUL, March quarter 2026).
Fast-growing digital channels: e-commerce value +57.7% and ITC quick commerce sales +57% (NielsenIQ; ITC).
Modern trade expansion: volume up 17.5% in Q2 2026 (NielsenIQ).
Government push on processing: PLI sales of ₹1,08,854 crore and jobs above target (PIB).
challenges: Weak volumes: market volume fell 2% and 68% of categories lost volume in April-June 2026 (NielsenIQ).
Rural slowdown: rural volumes down 5% while urban rose only 0.1% (NielsenIQ).
Corner shops losing volume: traditional trade down 6%, which hurts the biggest distribution network (NielsenIQ).
Cost volatility: HUL cited commodity and currency volatility from geopolitical tension and 'calibrated pricing actions' (HUL).
Price-led value growth: value rose 0.8% only because price rose 2.8% while volumes fell (NielsenIQ).
Mass skin care stayed subdued even as premium grew (HUL, March quarter 2026).

players.structure: A few large listed groups sell through a huge small-shop network. HUL turnover was ₹16,207 crore in one quarter and ITC FMCG was ₹24,210 crore in FY26; ITC alone reaches about 7 million outlets. The names below are well-known FMCG and retail employers, not a ranking by size; only HUL and ITC figures were verified here.

opsAngle: Last-mile reach is the moat: ITC serves about 7 million outlets, so route design, stockist fill rates and delivery frequency decide availability (ITC, FY26).
Channel-specific supply: modern trade (+17.5% volume), e-commerce and dark stores need different pack sizes, order patterns and replenishment than corner shops (NielsenIQ).
Volume is falling while price is rising: with volume -2% and price +2.8%, plants run below plan and every cost-saving and pack-mix decision matters (NielsenIQ).
Cost shocks: HUL points to commodity and currency volatility; hedging, supplier diversification and local sourcing cut risk (HUL).
Automation in warehousing: ITC runs 12 integrated facilities plus automated centres to optimise inventory (ITC, FY26).
Demand sensing matters most after the GST cut: price changes shift demand quickly, so forecast and inventory policy must adjust within weeks (GST Council release).
Premium and fast-moving mixes behave differently: premium lines are low-volume and high-margin, so SKU rationalisation and shelf-space trade-offs matter (HUL).
gdQuestions: Kirana stores are losing volume while quick commerce booms: should FMCG companies back the corner shop or the dark store?
Volumes fell 2% while prices rose 2.8%: is FMCG growth healthy or just inflation?
Did the GST cut on everyday goods help consumers or companies more?
Rural volumes are down 5%: is rural India still the growth engine for FMCG?
Should FMCG firms launch smaller, cheaper packs or push premium products?
Is a 100% FDI-open single-brand retail policy enough, or should multi-brand retail also open up?
How should an FMCG supply chain differ for quick commerce and general trade?
Does the food processing PLI scheme create real manufacturing champions or just subsidised sales?
Will large companies' own quick-commerce and direct-to-consumer channels hurt their distributors?
How should FMCG companies protect margins against commodity and currency volatility without hurting volume?
